title: Design a Multi-Tenant Enterprise AI Platform (AI Architect)

teaser.setup: You're the architect. Leadership wants one AI platform that many internal teams (and later, external customers) build on: shared retrieval, agents, and model access — governed and cost-attributed. Design it and defend the hard trade-offs.
you_will_practice: Tenant isolation and where you draw the boundary
Model strategy and routing across teams
Governance, cost attribution, and noisy-neighbor control
Scale, DR, and build-vs-buy under challenge

sample_node.prompt: How do you isolate tenants' data and retrieval?
sample_node.model: Prefer logical isolation with enforced tenant scoping (a tenant_id on every row/vector + policies that filter every query), with physical isolation (separate stores/keys) reserved for tenants with hard compliance needs. Trade-off: physical-per-tenant is safest but costly and operationally heavy; shared-with-enforced-scoping scales but you must guarantee the filter is never bypassed.

n1.prompt: Before any diagram: what do you clarify, and what's your platform's shape in a paragraph?
n1.model: Clarify: how many tenants/teams, internal-only or external too, data-residency/compliance, expected traffic skew, latency bars, and who owns cost. Shape: a shared control plane (auth, routing, guardrails, observability, quotas) over per-tenant-scoped data planes (retrieval indexes, agent state), with a model gateway abstracting providers. Tenants get isolation + quotas; the platform team owns governance, cost, and reliability.
signals: separates control plane from tenant data plane

n2.prompt: How do you isolate tenants' data and retrieval?

options.label: Shared store, tenant_id filter enforced by policy
Trust the app layer to scope queries
options.note: risky — one bug leaks across tenants

n2b.prompt: Defend or correct that isolation choice under compliance pressure.
n2b.model: App-layer-only scoping is unsafe — a single query bug crosses tenants; enforce isolation at the data layer (row/vector policies keyed on tenant, or separate stores). Physical-per-tenant is the safest but is costly and operationally heavy, so reserve it for tenants with hard compliance/residency needs and use enforced logical scoping for the rest. Never rely on the prompt or app code alone.
signals: isolation enforced at the data layer

n3.prompt: Teams have very different workloads. What's your model strategy across the platform?
n3.model: A model gateway with routing: cheap/fast models for high-volume simple calls, strong models for hard reasoning, per-team policy + quotas. Abstract the provider so you can add/swap models and fail over. Governed model allowlist (no team calls an unvetted model). Justify routing with per-class eval sets, not preference.

n4.prompt: One tenant's batch job floods the platform and everyone slows down. What prevents this?
n4.model: Per-tenant quotas + rate limits at the gateway; fair-scheduling / separate queues so a batch tenant can't starve interactive ones; concurrency caps and backpressure; isolate heavy async workloads onto their own capacity. Monitor per-tenant usage and alert on spikes. Noisy-neighbor control is a platform responsibility, not each app's.

n5.prompt: How do you govern this so security and compliance sign off?
n5.model: Identity flows through from the tenant's IdP; retrieval enforces per-user/tenant access; audit every model + tool call; data classification + masking; secrets in a manager; egress controls; treat retrieved/tool content as data not instructions. Central guardrails (input/output scanning) applied at the gateway so every tenant inherits them. A documented threat model per boundary.

n6.prompt: Finance wants each team billed for what they use, and total cost predictable. How?
n6.model: Meter at the gateway: tokens + model tier + retrieval/rerank per request, tagged by tenant/team → chargeback/showback dashboards. Levers: routing, prompt caching, quotas, cap max tokens. Budget alerts per tenant. Cost becomes attributable and controllable instead of one opaque bill. State assumptions (model mix, cache hit rate) when giving a forecast.

n7.prompt: How does it scale, and what's the DR story when a region or the model provider fails?
n7.model: Scale the stateless control plane + gateway horizontally; the model + vector store are the throughput bottlenecks — size/route accordingly. DR: multi-AZ, an alternate model provider/region as failover behind the gateway, backups of indexes + config, and a documented runbook. Test failover, don't assume it. SLOs per tier with alerting.

n8.prompt: The CTO asks: 'Should we build this platform at all, or buy?' Defend your recommendation.
n8.model: The architect move is to challenge the premise with TCO + strategic fit, not default to build. Buy/managed where it's undifferentiated (model hosting, vector store, observability); build the thin differentiated layer (governance, routing policy, tenant isolation, cost attribution) that's specific to us. Consider lock-in, compliance, and team capacity. Decide deliberately with a 1-2 year TCO view, not by reflex.

n9.prompt: Where did you draw a box without naming the boundary, the trade-off, or how you'd verify it?
checklist: I enforced tenant isolation at the data layer
I justified model routing with eval, not preference
I controlled noisy neighbors with quotas + isolation
I made cost attributable per tenant
I gave a tested DR story, not an assumed one
I reasoned build-vs-buy on TCO, not reflex

recommend.label: Keep Asking Why — system design chain
